summary: Triclofos sodium is a chloral-derivative sedative-hypnotic that is metabolised to the active CNS depressant trichloroethanol. It is used for short-term treatment of insomnia and, especially, as oral sedation in children for procedures such as EEG, MRI/CT imaging, and dental/ophthalmic examinations, where it is generally better tolerated (less gastric irritation) than chloral hydrate. It is NOT FDA-approved; this record is based on the UK SmPC/BNF and other reference sources and is pending clinical review. Doses are typically expressed as triclofos sodium (1 g triclofos approximates ~600 mg chloral hydrate equivalent). It should be used short-term because of tolerance and dependence, avoided with alcohol and other CNS depressants, and avoided in marked hepatic or renal impairment; overdose causes respiratory depression and arrhythmia.
indications: Sedation for diagnostic or minor procedures in children (e.g. EEG, MRI/CT imaging, audiometry, ophthalmic/dental examination)

dosage.d: 1 g to 2 g (triclofos sodium) at bedtime
250-500 mg (commonly weight-based ~25-30 mg/kg, up to ~50-70 mg/kg for procedural sedation per local protocols)
dosage.n: Follow institutional procedural-sedation protocol with monitoring

dosage.d: Specialist use only - dose per neonatal/paediatric protocol with respiratory monitoring
dosage.n: Risk of respiratory depression; use cautiously

admin: Give orally, well diluted with water, milk, or fruit juice to reduce gastric irritation and mask taste
For procedural sedation in children, administer ~30-45 minutes before the procedure under appropriate monitoring
Have facilities for monitoring sedation depth, oxygen saturation, and airway support available
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time
moa: Triclofos sodium is a prodrug rapidly metabolised (largely by hepatic and gut phosphatases/dehydrogenase) to trichloroethanol, the active moiety responsible for its hypnotic effect. Trichloroethanol is a general central nervous system depressant; like chloral hydrate it is thought to potentiate GABA-A receptor-mediated chloride conductance and depress neuronal excitability, producing dose-dependent sedation, hypnosis, and (at high doses) respiratory and cardiovascular depression. Compared with chloral hydrate, triclofos releases trichloroethanol without the gastric-irritant chloral hydrate itself, improving GI tolerability.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to triclofos, chloral derivatives, or excipients
Severe cardiac disease / serious cardiac arrhythmia
Gastritis or active peptic ulcer disease (gastric irritation)
relative: Respiratory insufficiency / sleep apnoea (respiratory depression risk)
History of drug or alcohol dependence
Elderly and debilitated patients (increased sensitivity, falls)
monitor: Respiratory rate and oxygen saturation (especially in children and the elderly)
Signs of tolerance or dependence with repeated use
Cardiac status in those with arrhythmia risk

preg: Safety in pregnancy has not been established and chloral derivatives cross the placenta. Triclofos is not recommended during pregnancy; use only if considered essential and no safer alternative exists, particularly avoiding use near term because of the risk of neonatal CNS/respiratory depression.
lact: Trichloroethanol (the active metabolite of chloral derivatives) is excreted in breast milk and sedation/drowsiness has been reported in breastfed infants. Avoid use during breastfeeding, or interrupt breastfeeding if a dose is required.
renal: Trichloroethanol and its metabolites are eliminated via the kidney (largely as the glucuronide). Avoid triclofos in marked renal impairment because of accumulation of active metabolite and risk of excessive sedation; use cautiously and at reduced dose in milder impairment.
hepatic: The liver activates triclofos to trichloroethanol and conjugates it for excretion. Avoid in marked hepatic impairment due to altered metabolism, accumulation, and increased sensitivity to CNS depression.

major: Alcohol and other CNS depressants - opioids, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, sedating antihistamines (severe additive sedation/respiratory depression)
Anticoagulants e.g. warfarin (transient displacement and enhanced anticoagulant effect - monitor INR)
moderate: IV furosemide given after chloral derivatives (sweating, flushing, blood-pressure changes)
Other drugs causing arrhythmia (additive cardiac risk)
interactions.food: Take with or after food and well diluted to reduce gastric irritation
interactions.alcohol: Avoid completely - dangerous additive CNS and respiratory depression (the historical 'Mickey Finn' interaction with chloral)
interactions.diagnostics: Chloral derivatives can cause false-positive urinary glucose tests (copper-reduction methods) and may interfere with urinary catecholamine and 17-hydroxycorticosteroid assays

serious: Respiratory depression (especially in children, elderly, or with other CNS depressants)
Dependence and tolerance with prolonged use
Severe withdrawal on abrupt cessation after chronic use

monitoring: Depth of sedation and conscious level
Respiratory rate and oxygen saturation, especially in children during procedural sedation and in the elderly
Cardiac rhythm in patients at arrhythmia risk and in overdose
Evidence of tolerance, dependence, or rebound insomnia with continued use
Falls risk and residual daytime sedation
counsel: This medicine makes you sleepy - do not drive or operate machinery until you know how it affects you
Do not drink alcohol while taking it
Take it well diluted with water/juice and with food to avoid stomach upset
It is for short-term use only; do not increase the dose or use it long-term without advice (risk of dependence)
Do not stop suddenly after prolonged use - withdrawal can occur
Keep well out of reach of children; overdose is dangerous
Tell your doctor about other sedating medicines, liver or kidney problems, and pregnancy/breastfeeding
pk: Active metabolite trichloroethanol peaks within ~1-2 hours
Trichloroethanol half-life approximately 8-12 hours (longer in neonates and in hepatic/renal impairment)
Store below 25 degrees C; protect from light; keep liquid tightly closed
pearls: NOT FDA-approved; this record is based on the UK SmPC/BNF and other references and is pending clinical review.
Triclofos is a prodrug of trichloroethanol (the same active metabolite as chloral hydrate) but causes less gastric irritation - hence its main use as oral paediatric procedural sedation (EEG/MRI/CT).
Doses are expressed as triclofos sodium; ~1 g triclofos is roughly equivalent to ~600 mg chloral hydrate.
Short-term use only - tolerance and dependence develop; never combine with alcohol or other CNS depressants.
Avoid in marked hepatic or renal impairment and in severe cardiac disease/arrhythmia.
Procedural sedation in children requires appropriate monitoring (SpO2, airway support) because of the risk of respiratory depression; can cause false-positive urinary glucose tests.
missed: Triclofos is normally taken only when needed (for sleep or before a procedure), so a regular missed-dose schedule does not usually apply. If prescribed at bedtime and a dose is missed, skip it rather than taking it late in the night; do not take a double dose.
overdose: Overdose causes deep CNS depression progressing to coma, respiratory depression, hypotension, hypothermia, miosis, and potentially serious cardiac arrhythmias (chloral derivatives sensitise the myocardium to catecholamines). Management is supportive: secure the airway and support ventilation, give activated charcoal if early and airway protected, monitor cardiac rhythm continuously, and treat arrhythmias cautiously (beta-blockers such as propranolol/esmolol for catecholamine-sensitised tachyarrhythmias; avoid catecholamines where possible). Haemodialysis can remove trichloroethanol in severe poisoning. Manage hypotension with fluids/inotropes.
